title: CSS Selectors
summary: A CSS selector chooses which page parts a rule should change.
introduction: A CSS selector chooses which page parts a rule should change. Think of calling out a team name in class. A selector can choose all paragraphs, one class of boxes or one element with an id.
learningObjectives: Select elements by type, class, id and attribute
Combine selectors with descendant, child and sibling combinators

rows: Every element with that tag name
Elements whose `class` attribute contains the name
Elements that have an attribute, or one with a given value

blocks.text: Simple selectors can be chained without spaces to require all of them at once: `button.primary` matches buttons that have the class `primary`, and `.card.featured` matches elements that have both classes. Classes are the workhorse of CSS because you can put the same class on any number of elements and combine several on one element. Ids must be unique on the page and carry a lot of weight in the cascade, so most teams reserve them for fragment links and JavaScript and style with classes.

blocks.text: A combinator joins two selectors and describes how the matched elements relate in the tree. The difference between a descendant and a child combinator is the one that matters most in practice: `.menu a` reaches *every* link anywhere inside the menu, including links inside nested sub-menus, while `.menu > a` only reaches links that are direct children.

blocks.text: Every link is blue because the descendant combinator reaches into the nested list, but only *Products* and *About* are bold: the child combinator stops at direct children, and the nested links sit inside a second `ul` and `li`, so `.menu > li > a` never reaches them. Whenever a rule applies to more elements than you expected, check whether a descendant combinator should have been a child combinator.

items: `[lang|="en"]` the value is `en` or starts with `en-`

blocks.title: Marking external links and PDF downloads

blocks.text: A comma groups selectors that share declarations. Three functions make such lists shorter and safer. `:is()` matches if any selector inside it matches, so `article :is(h1, h2, h3)` replaces three descendant selectors. `:not()` excludes elements. `:where()` works like `:is()` but adds no specificity, which makes it ideal for base styles that components should be able to override. And `:has()` selects an element based on what is *inside* it, the "parent selector" that CSS lacked for twenty years and that all major browsers support.

blocks.title: Over-specific selectors
blocks.text: Selectors like `div#main .content ul li a` are fragile (any change to the markup breaks them) and extremely specific, so a plain `.link` class written later cannot override them and you end up reaching for `!important`. Give the element a class and select it with that alone; keep selectors as short as the design allows.

blocks.title: Naming classes
blocks.text: Name classes after what the element *is* or *does*, not how it looks: `.alert-danger` still makes sense when the design changes from red to orange, `.red-text` does not. Use lowercase words joined by hyphens, and keep a class to one component or one purpose.

questions.question: Which selector matches a paragraph that comes *immediately after* an `h2` with the same parent?
questions.explanation: `+` is the next-sibling combinator. `h2 p` would need the paragraph inside the heading, `h2 > p` directly inside it, and `h2 ~ p` matches any later sibling, not only the immediate one.

questions.question: `.card:has(img)` selects the images inside cards.
questions.explanation: `:has()` selects the element *before* it, the card, when something inside matches. To select the images you would write `.card img`.
